evidence.asserts: The layer returns its declared envelope on BOTH paths, success and failure, and a caller can tell which without parsing prose. Proven by a registered gate that probes the LIVE gateway rather than by reading source: http_envelope issues real requests as anon, as a member and with no key, and asserts that error bodies carry all four envelope keys and that the HTTP status agrees with the body. A structural check - does the function import _shared/envelope.ts - would be the wrong prover here and R6 would refuse it, because importing the module is not the same as returning the envelope when the path fails.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: PASS - the envelope and the status agree with the body on all 40 relations probed. The gate also measures the harder half and reports it rather than hiding it: 27 of those relations CANNOT distinguish refusal from absence, which is PostgREST + RLS by construction rather than a defect patchable at the relation. What makes that acceptable is that every page reading them answers the question at its own layer, and the gate counts how: redirects-unauthenticated x19, anon-by-design x2, settles-auth-before-reads x1. A prover returning a bare PASS over 40 relations while 27 were structurally ambiguous would assert more than it measured. depends_on names the subject artifacts as well as the gate, so a change to the functions or migrations under this claim still expires it; replay re-earns it in one command.

findings.title: WITHDRAWN - gateway/DB envelope evidence does not cover the L1 layer
findings.detail: FALSE GREEN WITHDRAWN BY ME, SAME SESSION, BEFORE ANYONE RELIED ON IT. I measured the PostgREST response envelope at the gateway - six classes, including the decisive authenticated-but-forbidden case - and then banked EVERY owed status_body_agreement row on the page regardless of which LAYER it belongs to. That was an over-claim. This oracle is per-layer, and the layers are distinct subjects: L1 is the page's own CLIENT code, L2 here is EDGE FUNCTIONS or the gateway depending on the page, L3 is the DB, L4 is AI / cron / realtime / print. My probe exercised the database's envelope surfaced through REST - the codes are Postgres codes (42501, 42703) and PGRST parse errors. It says NOTHING about whether an edge function returns a status matching its body, whether the client's own error handling agrees with what it received, or whether an AI path does. Keeping this green would have been the exact failure this bank exists to prevent: evidence that is real but does not cover the claim. The DB-layer row keeps its green because that IS what was measured; this row returns to owed. TO FINISH for THIS layer: probe the layer's own error envelope. For an edge function, invoke it with a deliberately bad payload and compare the HTTP status against the body it returns - now possible since supabase_edge_runtime_workhive was started this session after being down 17 hours. For the client layer, intercept a known status and assert what the page RENDERS agrees with it. Row stays owed.
findings.observed: layer subject: L1 (client (pre-body auth swap + render))

evidence.asserts: The HTTP status and the body agree: no 200 carrying an error, no 4xx carrying a success. Proven by a registered gate that probes the LIVE gateway rather than by reading source - http_envelope issues real requests as anon, as a member and with no key, and asserts the status matches what the body actually says. This is the behavioural half of the envelope contract and cannot be settled structurally: a function can import the envelope helper and still answer 200 with an error inside, which is precisely the shape that makes a failed read look like an empty one to every caller downstream.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: PASS - status and body agree on all 40 relations probed, across anon, member and no-key callers. The gate reports what it cannot settle instead of smoothing it: 27 relations cannot distinguish refusal from absence, PostgREST + RLS by construction, each answered at the page layer rather than the relation (redirects-unauthenticated x19, anon-by-design x2, settles-auth-before-reads x1). That distinction matters more for THIS oracle than most, because a 200 carrying zero rows is exactly how a refusal disguises itself as an absence - the same class this platform hit when a failed read rendered as 'no contacts saved yet', and when a zero-row update returned no error and a reporter was told their report had been sent. depends_on names the subject artifacts as well as the prover, so a migration beneath the claim still expires it - as it did within this same session, when migration ...000068 landed after these rows were first banked and correctly staled the ones resting on migrations.
evidence.value_checked: gate:http_envelope | PASS: status agrees with body on all 40 relations | probed live as anon / member / no-key | 27 relations structurally cannot separate refusal from absence (PostgREST+RLS), answered per page: redirects-unauthenticated x19, anon-by-design x2, settles-auth-before-reads x1 | depends_on: index.html, tools/prove_http_envelope.py, utils.js

scenarios.oracle: the same call twice produces ONE effect; the second is refused or absorbed, and the count in the DB proves which

evidence.asserts: The same ordered read, issued twice over two SEPARATE connections, returns the same bytes: a repeat read is not quietly a different read. Proven by a registered gate rather than a session - read_idempotency re-issues every repeatable read on the platform and compares a digest that is itself proven sensitive, so a match means agreement rather than a digest too coarse to notice a difference.
evidence.checked: Run live this session across all 22 pages: 93 repeatable reads, PASS - every repeatable read returned identical bytes across two separate connections. The sub-verdicts are carried here rather than flattened into the headline: 83 plain idempotent, 5 idempotent-uncontrolled (repeatable, but with no control proving the digest would have caught a change), 2 idempotent-modulo-clock, 2 CONTROL-FAILED and 1 UNKNOWN. Those last three are not passes and are recorded as such - a row claiming clean green while 3 reads never produced a verdict would be the vacuous match this gate exists to refuse.
evidence.value_checked: gate:read_idempotency | 93 repeatable reads across 22 pages, PASS | idempotent 83, uncontrolled 5, modulo-clock 2, control-failed 2, unknown 1 | digest proven sensitive | depends_on: index.html, tools/prove_read_idempotency.py, utils.js

scenarios.question: does each layer this page rests on honour its own contract - envelope, status/body agreement, idempotency, total ordering, declared units?
scenarios.oracle: a paginated or sorted read has a TOTAL order - re-running it does not reshuffle equal keys, so page 2 cannot repeat or skip a row from page 1

evidence.asserts: A paginated or sorted read at this layer has a TOTAL order: re-running it returns the same rows in the same sequence, so no row appears on two pages and none is skipped. Proven by a REGISTERED gate rather than a session - paginated-order-totality scans every paged-and-ordered query chain on the platform and fails if one ends without a unique tiebreaker, holding forward-only at 0. R2 turns this row INVALID rather than silently green if that gate is deleted or renamed.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: 176 paginated+ordered chains scanned platform-wide, 0 non-total, ratchet PASS at 0, and the gate's selftest passes BOTH directions - it catches a non-total order and accepts a tiebreakered one, which separates a working scanner from one that approves everything. The run also caught a regression introduced earlier in this same session (report-sender.html loadBounces ordering on triggered_at with no tiebreaker, 0 -> 1), fixed to .order('id') and back to 0. depends_on names the SUBJECT artifacts as well as the gate: anchoring to the gate alone was refused by R7, correctly - a page or migration that changes the query must expire the claim about it. Gate-backing buys a one-command recovery via replay, not immunity from staleness.
evidence.value_checked: gate:paginated-order-totality | 176 chains scanned, 0 non-total, forward-only PASS | selftest both directions | caught+fixed this session: report-sender.html:1357 order(triggered_at) | depends_on: index.html, tools/validate_paginated_order_totality.py, utils.js

scenarios.question: does each layer this page rests on honour its own contract - envelope, status/body agreement, idempotency, total ordering, declared units?
scenarios.oracle: the value carries its unit at the boundary (pesos vs credits vs percent vs whole-percent) - the class that made a knob of 10 mean 1000%

evidence.asserts: A value carries its unit AT THE BOUNDARY - pesos vs credits vs percent vs whole-percent - so no consumer has to infer the scale. This is the class the oracle names as having made a knob of 10 mean 1000%. Proven by a registered gate: units_at_boundary requires every money, credit, percent and duration column to declare its unit by CHECK, comment, sibling unit column or name, and fails outright if any column mixes two scales.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: PASS WITH DEBT, and the debt is recorded rather than rounded off. MIXED-SCALE = 0, the hard invariant that produces the 10-means-1000% failure. Two columns carry their unit only by convention and are reported, not failed: conversation_analytics.answer_quality_rating (percent) and service_credit_ledger.amount (money), each with no CHECK, no comment, no sibling unit column and a name that does not say; five more are undecl-latent. Those seven are real debt against this oracle and are named so they can be closed rather than rediscovered. The gate was matched to the oracle deliberately: the oracle says the value carries its unit AT THE BOUNDARY and names the mixed-scale failure, which is this gate's subject - the neighbouring prove_units_visible answers a different question (what a reader sees) and would have been the wrong prover.
evidence.value_checked: gate:units_at_boundary | MIXED-SCALE 0 (the hard invariant) | UNDECLARED 2: conversation_analytics.answer_quality_rating (percent), service_credit_ledger.amount (money) | undecl-latent 5 | PASS with debt | depends_on: index.html, tools/prove_units_at_boundary.py, utils.js

scenarios.oracle: the layer returns its declared envelope on BOTH paths - success and failure - and a caller can tell which without parsing prose

evidence.asserts: The layer returns its declared envelope on BOTH paths, success and failure, and a caller can tell which without parsing prose. Proven by a registered gate that probes the LIVE gateway rather than by reading source: http_envelope issues real requests as anon, as a member and with no key, and asserts that error bodies carry all four envelope keys and that the HTTP status agrees with the body. A structural check - does the function import _shared/envelope.ts - would be the wrong prover here and R6 would refuse it, because importing the module is not the same as returning the envelope when the path fails.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: PASS - the envelope and the status agree with the body on all 40 relations probed. The gate also measures the harder half and reports it rather than hiding it: 27 of those relations CANNOT distinguish refusal from absence, which is PostgREST + RLS by construction rather than a defect patchable at the relation. What makes that acceptable is that every page reading them answers the question at its own layer, and the gate counts how: redirects-unauthenticated x19, anon-by-design x2, settles-auth-before-reads x1. A prover returning a bare PASS over 40 relations while 27 were structurally ambiguous would assert more than it measured. depends_on names the subject artifacts as well as the gate, so a change to the functions or migrations under this claim still expires it; replay re-earns it in one command.

evidence.asserts: The HTTP status and the body agree: no 200 carrying an error, no 4xx carrying a success. Proven by a registered gate that probes the LIVE gateway rather than by reading source - http_envelope issues real requests as anon, as a member and with no key, and asserts the status matches what the body actually says. This is the behavioural half of the envelope contract and cannot be settled structurally: a function can import the envelope helper and still answer 200 with an error inside, which is precisely the shape that makes a failed read look like an empty one to every caller downstream.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: PASS - status and body agree on all 40 relations probed, across anon, member and no-key callers. The gate reports what it cannot settle instead of smoothing it: 27 relations cannot distinguish refusal from absence, PostgREST + RLS by construction, each answered at the page layer rather than the relation (redirects-unauthenticated x19, anon-by-design x2, settles-auth-before-reads x1). That distinction matters more for THIS oracle than most, because a 200 carrying zero rows is exactly how a refusal disguises itself as an absence - the same class this platform hit when a failed read rendered as 'no contacts saved yet', and when a zero-row update returned no error and a reporter was told their report had been sent. depends_on names the subject artifacts as well as the prover, so a migration beneath the claim still expires it - as it did within this same session, when migration ...000068 landed after these rows were first banked and correctly staled the ones resting on migrations.

findings.title: banked green for a non-HTTP layer on evidence taken only at the PostgREST gateway - the edge envelope is demonstrably a different shape
findings.detail: I banked envelope_shape and status_body_agreement for EVERY layer subject on one measurement: real GETs against http://127.0.0.1:54321/rest/v1. That measurement is sound for the client/gateway/db layers and says NOTHING about this row's layer. The proof that it is a different question, taken minutes later once the edge runtime was restarted: POST {} to /functions/v1/ai-gateway answers 400 with the body {"error":"Missing agent"} - ONE key. The PostgREST envelope this row was banked on is {code, message, details, hint} - FOUR keys, and the row's own evidence asserts all four are present. So the edge layer does not satisfy the property this row was marked green for, and if it had been probed the verdict might well have been a finding. HOW IT HAPPENED: the banker iterated every CA layer row on the page and applied the same gateway result to all of them, using R7/page_layer_deps to get the DEPENDENCIES right while never checking that the MEASUREMENT matched the layer. Correct anchoring on the wrong evidence still yields a false green - an oracle that does not match its claim. AND THE EDGE RUNTIME WAS DOWN THE WHOLE TIME: supabase_edge_runtime_workhive had been 'Exited (255) 4 days ago', so at the moment of banking every edge function on the platform was answering 503. A layer claim banked while that layer is not running cannot be anything but false, and nothing in the banker noticed - the reading came from a different service that WAS up. `docker start` brought it back and it now serves 58 functions. TO RE-EARN: probe the layer this row actually names. For edge/ai/external-send that is /functions/v1/<fn> with apikey + a member JWT (tools/backend_edge_probe.py has the helpers; note its anon_key() returns '' on this stack because it only accepts legacy eyJ JWTs - prove_http_envelope.resolve_key() carries the working fallback). For cron/realtime/print/cdn the envelope question needs its own instrument and the row should stay owed until one exists, rather than inheriting a reading from whatever service happened to answer.

withdrawn_evidence.asserts: every response this page's reads receive carries the envelope shape its client expects
withdrawn_evidence.checked: PASSES. Of this page's 13 read relation(s), 3 were probed live at the gateway (early_access_emails, pm_assets, pm_completions).  PLATFORM RESULT: across 40 relations, ZERO envelope defects and ZERO status/body disagreements. The error envelope is well-formed - {code, message, details, hint} on every error body, 400 (not 500) for an unknown column, 406 with PGRST116 for a single-object read of 0 rows, and a Content-Range header whenever Prefer: count=exact is asked. The status always agrees with the body: no 2xx carries an error object and no 4xx omits a machine-readable code. HOW IT WAS MEASURED: real HTTP GETs against the LIVE local gateway (http://127.0.0.1:54321/rest/v1), 40 relations, as three personas - anonymous with the publishable key, an AUTHENTICATED member (a real minted JWT for the seeded test identity), and a request carrying NO apikey at all. GET only, so nothing is written and there is nothing to roll back. Per relation: a collection read; the same read authenticated; the same read unauthenticated; a single-object read (Accept: application/vnd.pgrst.object+json) of a row that cannot exist; a read naming a column that does not exist; and a Prefer: count=exact read. THREE NON-VACUITY CONTROLS, all passing, because a gateway that answered 200 to everything would make every verdict here free: (1) an unknown column MUST return 400 - proves the prober can observe a failure at all; (2) community_posts MUST return rows to an ANON caller, since it is the public feed - proves anon is not blanket-denied, so a 200 [] on a tenant table is RLS working rather than a dead key; (3) authenticated MUST out-read anon somewhere - without it, 'a refusal looks like absence' would be vacuously true. AND THE PROBE'S OWN FIRST RUN REPORTED TWO DEFECTS THAT WERE BOTH MINE, corrected before anything was banked. It probed ?id=eq.<uuid> on every relation, but community_xp is keyed (worker_name, hive_id) and has no id column, so the request returned 42703 'column does not exist' - my malformed query read back as the gateway's misbehaviour. And it treated projects' 42501 'insufficient privilege' as a shape violation when a refusal carrying a machine-readable code is a CORRECT envelope - on this platform it is the better behaviour. A probe that assumes a schema it never checked produces findings about itself. THESE ROWS WERE OWED ON A FALSE PREMISE, and that is worth recording because the premise was in our OWN TOOLING. Two provers documented that these oracles 'need the REST gateway, which is not reachable from this shell (kong publishes no host port)', and one copied that sentence into banked evidence. It was wrong: docker ps shows supabase_kong_workhive 0.0.0.0:54321->8000/tcp, and one curl with the publishable key answers 200. A ceiling written into a tool's docstring stops reading like a claim and starts reading like documentation, so it survived across sessions and kept ~130 rows owed. Corrected in place in both files rather than deleted.

findings.title: WITHDRAWN - gateway/DB envelope evidence does not cover the L4 layer
findings.detail: FALSE GREEN WITHDRAWN BY ME, SAME SESSION, BEFORE ANYONE RELIED ON IT. I measured the PostgREST response envelope at the gateway - six classes, including the decisive authenticated-but-forbidden case - and then banked EVERY owed status_body_agreement row on the page regardless of which LAYER it belongs to. That was an over-claim. This oracle is per-layer, and the layers are distinct subjects: L1 is the page's own CLIENT code, L2 here is EDGE FUNCTIONS or the gateway depending on the page, L3 is the DB, L4 is AI / cron / realtime / print. My probe exercised the database's envelope surfaced through REST - the codes are Postgres codes (42501, 42703) and PGRST parse errors. It says NOTHING about whether an edge function returns a status matching its body, whether the client's own error handling agrees with what it received, or whether an AI path does. Keeping this green would have been the exact failure this bank exists to prevent: evidence that is real but does not cover the claim. The DB-layer row keeps its green because that IS what was measured; this row returns to owed. TO FINISH for THIS layer: probe the layer's own error envelope. For an edge function, invoke it with a deliberately bad payload and compare the HTTP status against the body it returns - now possible since supabase_edge_runtime_workhive was started this session after being down 17 hours. For the client layer, intercept a known status and assert what the page RENDERS agrees with it. Row stays owed.

findings.detail: I banked envelope_shape and status_body_agreement for EVERY layer subject on one measurement: real GETs against http://127.0.0.1:54321/rest/v1. That measurement is sound for the client/gateway/db layers and says NOTHING about this row's layer. The proof that it is a different question, taken minutes later once the edge runtime was restarted: POST {} to /functions/v1/ai-gateway answers 400 with the body {"error":"Missing agent"} - ONE key. The PostgREST envelope this row was banked on is {code, message, details, hint} - FOUR keys, and the row's own evidence asserts all four are present. So the edge layer does not satisfy the property this row was marked green for, and if it had been probed the verdict might well have been a finding. HOW IT HAPPENED: the banker iterated every CA layer row on the page and applied the same gateway result to all of them, using R7/page_layer_deps to get the DEPENDENCIES right while never checking that the MEASUREMENT matched the layer. Correct anchoring on the wrong evidence still yields a false green - an oracle that does not match its claim. AND THE EDGE RUNTIME WAS DOWN THE WHOLE TIME: supabase_edge_runtime_workhive had been 'Exited (255) 4 days ago', so at the moment of banking every edge function on the platform was answering 503. A layer claim banked while that layer is not running cannot be anything but false, and nothing in the banker noticed - the reading came from a different service that WAS up. `docker start` brought it back and it now serves 58 functions. TO RE-EARN: probe the layer this row actually names. For edge/ai/external-send that is /functions/v1/<fn> with apikey + a member JWT (tools/backend_edge_probe.py has the helpers; note its anon_key() returns '' on this stack because it only accepts legacy eyJ JWTs - prove_http_envelope.resolve_key() carries the working fallback). For cron/realtime/print/cdn the envelope question needs its own instrument and the row should stay owed until one exists, rather than inheriting a reading from whatever service happened to answer.

withdrawn_evidence.asserts: the HTTP status always agrees with the body: no success carries an error and no error omits its code
withdrawn_evidence.checked: PASSES. Of this page's 13 read relation(s), 3 were probed live at the gateway (early_access_emails, pm_assets, pm_completions).  PLATFORM RESULT: across 40 relations, ZERO envelope defects and ZERO status/body disagreements. The error envelope is well-formed - {code, message, details, hint} on every error body, 400 (not 500) for an unknown column, 406 with PGRST116 for a single-object read of 0 rows, and a Content-Range header whenever Prefer: count=exact is asked. The status always agrees with the body: no 2xx carries an error object and no 4xx omits a machine-readable code. HOW IT WAS MEASURED: real HTTP GETs against the LIVE local gateway (http://127.0.0.1:54321/rest/v1), 40 relations, as three personas - anonymous with the publishable key, an AUTHENTICATED member (a real minted JWT for the seeded test identity), and a request carrying NO apikey at all. GET only, so nothing is written and there is nothing to roll back. Per relation: a collection read; the same read authenticated; the same read unauthenticated; a single-object read (Accept: application/vnd.pgrst.object+json) of a row that cannot exist; a read naming a column that does not exist; and a Prefer: count=exact read. THREE NON-VACUITY CONTROLS, all passing, because a gateway that answered 200 to everything would make every verdict here free: (1) an unknown column MUST return 400 - proves the prober can observe a failure at all; (2) community_posts MUST return rows to an ANON caller, since it is the public feed - proves anon is not blanket-denied, so a 200 [] on a tenant table is RLS working rather than a dead key; (3) authenticated MUST out-read anon somewhere - without it, 'a refusal looks like absence' would be vacuously true. AND THE PROBE'S OWN FIRST RUN REPORTED TWO DEFECTS THAT WERE BOTH MINE, corrected before anything was banked. It probed ?id=eq.<uuid> on every relation, but community_xp is keyed (worker_name, hive_id) and has no id column, so the request returned 42703 'column does not exist' - my malformed query read back as the gateway's misbehaviour. And it treated projects' 42501 'insufficient privilege' as a shape violation when a refusal carrying a machine-readable code is a CORRECT envelope - on this platform it is the better behaviour. A probe that assumes a schema it never checked produces findings about itself. THESE ROWS WERE OWED ON A FALSE PREMISE, and that is worth recording because the premise was in our OWN TOOLING. Two provers documented that these oracles 'need the REST gateway, which is not reachable from this shell (kong publishes no host port)', and one copied that sentence into banked evidence. It was wrong: docker ps shows supabase_kong_workhive 0.0.0.0:54321->8000/tcp, and one curl with the publishable key answers 200. A ceiling written into a tool's docstring stops reading like a claim and starts reading like documentation, so it survived across sessions and kept ~130 rows owed. Corrected in place in both files rather than deleted.

evidence.asserts: The HTTP status and the body agree: no 200 carrying an error, no 4xx carrying a success. Proven by a registered gate that probes the LIVE gateway rather than by reading source - http_envelope issues real requests as anon, as a member and with no key, and asserts the status matches what the body actually says. This is the behavioural half of the envelope contract and cannot be settled structurally: a function can import the envelope helper and still answer 200 with an error inside, which is precisely the shape that makes a failed read look like an empty one to every caller downstream.

The gate reports what it cannot settle instead of smoothing it: 27 relations cannot distinguish refusal from absence, PostgREST + RLS by construction, each answered at the page layer rather than the relation (redirects-unauthenticated x19, anon-by-design x2, settles-auth-before-reads x1). findings.title: MEASURED with tools/prove_write_atomicity.py, which asks the oracle's question in the two halves it actually has.
findings.detail: MEASURED with tools/prove_write_atomicity.py, which asks the oracle's question in the two halves it actually has. STRUCTURE - WHO SEQUENCES THE WRITE, read out of pg_trigger and pg_proc rather than guessed. A page that writes two tables through two awaited client calls has NO transaction around them: a 500, a closed laptop or a dead network between the two leaves the first applied and the second missing, and nothing errors afterwards. A page that writes one table and lets a TRIGGER or an RPC write the second is atomic by construction, because one statement is one transaction. LEDGER - WHETHER A HALF-WRITE IS VISIBLE TODAY: 14 of 14 declared conservation invariants were checked against live data and ALL HOLD - the inventory running balance, transactions with no orphan item, every reply and every live safety post carrying its XP award row, no XP row outliving a deleted post unreversed, no staged reservation both consumed and released, one AMC briefing per hive per shift date, a scope item not completed twice, no project child outliving its project. ★AND THE DETECTOR IS PROVEN ABLE TO SEE A LINK, which is what stops 'client-sequenced' from being a verdict about the tool: the control pair community_posts -> community_post_xp_awards is joined by the trigger handle_community_post_xp, and the detector finds it. A detector that cannot see that link cannot see any link, and would report every page as client-sequenced. ROSTER-WIDE: 11 pages client-sequenced, 11 single-or-no-write. FOR THIS PAGE THE STRUCTURE DOES NOT SATISFY THE ORACLE, so this is NOT banked green even though nothing is broken today. The page writes early_access_emails + worker_profiles and the database does NOT link them - no trigger, no single RPC that writes both. So the first clause of the oracle ('either lands whole or not at all') is false as a structural matter: a failure between the two client calls leaves the first applied and the second missing, silently. WHAT THE LEDGER SAYS IS THE OTHER HALF, and it is genuinely reassuring rather than decorative: every declared conservation invariant holds against live data, so no half-write has HAPPENED. But 'has not happened yet' is a statement about this dataset, not about the code - the same shape as a latent null-collapse that no row has triggered. Banking it green would convert an absence of evidence into a guarantee. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: either the second write moves behind a trigger or an RPC (making it atomic by construction, which is what 11 of the 22 pages already do and what the control pair demonstrates), or a probe interrupts the page BETWEEN the two calls and shows the ledger invariant catching the resulting half-state - which would prove the second clause with teeth instead of by absence. ★CORRECTION TO THE STRENGTH OF THIS CLAIM, made after reading what the pairs actually are. The prover enumerates every PAIR OF RELATIONS a page writes and asks whether the database links them - a cartesian over the page's write set, NOT a list of observed co-writes. Most of these pairs are therefore not one logical write split in two: community_posts + community_reactions are two separate user actions, asset_nodes + inventory_items are two different edits, and hive_audit_log pairs with everything because it is appended alongside many actions. A HALF-WRITE IS ONLY POSSIBLE WHERE A SINGLE ACTION WRITES BOTH TABLES, which is a smaller set than the pair count suggests - the plausible ones on this roster are flows where one submit genuinely lands two rows (resume_documents + resume_versions on an upload; logbook + schedule_items when a planned item is completed; asset_nodes + logbook when an asset is created during capture). Which pairs those are cannot be read from pg_trigger; it needs the page's write FUNCTIONS traced. SO THE ROW STAYS OWED FOR A NARROWER REASON THAN THE PAIR COUNT IMPLIES: the page writes multiple tables with no DB linkage, which MAY permit a half-write on whichever action writes two - and the ledger shows none has occurred. This is not a claim that every listed pair is a live risk, and the distinction is recorded rather than letting a large pair count read as a large defect. CONCRETE NEXT SLICE: not 'add triggers', but trace this page's write functions, identify which single actions write two tables, and interrupt only those between the calls.

A page writing one table and letting a TRIGGER or an RPC write the second is atomic BY CONSTRUCTION, because one statement is one transaction. LEDGER - WHETHER A HALF-WRITE IS VISIBLE TODAY: 14 of 14 declared conservation invariants checked against live data and ALL HOLD. ★AND THE DETECTOR IS PROVEN ABLE TO SEE A LINK, which is what stops 'client-sequenced' from being a verdict about the tool: the control pair community_posts -> community_post_xp_awards is joined by the trigger handle_community_post_xp and the detector finds it. evidence.checked: Run live this session: PASS - every rewrite on the way in belongs to a named class, and none of the 106 capped columns has ever truncated a stored value (widest: engineering_calcs.sow_text at 984 of 4000). The gate was right to stop it - it assigns NEW.x := OLD.x, a shape none of its four classes covered. STRUCTURE - WHO SEQUENCES THE WRITE, read out of pg_trigger and pg_proc rather than guessed: a page writing two tables through two awaited client calls has NO transaction around them, so a 500, a closed laptop or a dead network between them leaves the first applied and the second missing, and nothing errors afterwards. A page writing one table and letting a TRIGGER or an RPC write the second is atomic BY CONSTRUCTION, because one statement is one transaction. LEDGER - WHETHER A HALF-WRITE IS VISIBLE TODAY: 14 of 14 declared conservation invariants checked against live data and ALL HOLD. ★AND THE DETECTOR IS PROVEN ABLE TO SEE A LINK, which is what stops 'client-sequenced' from being a verdict about the tool: the control pair community_posts -> community_post_xp_awards is joined by the trigger handle_community_post_xp and the detector finds it. A detector that cannot see that link cannot see any link, and would report every page as client-sequenced. ★ROSTER: {"client-sequenced": 11, "single-or-no-write": 11}. FOR THIS PAGE THE STRUCTURE DOES NOT SATISFY THE ORACLE, so this is NOT green even though nothing is broken today. It writes early_access_emails + worker_profiles and the database does NOT link them - no trigger, no single RPC writing both - so a failure between the two client calls leaves the first applied and the second missing, silently. Every declared invariant holds against live data, which is genuinely reassuring, but 'has not happened yet' is a statement about this dataset, not about the code; banking it green would convert an absence of evidence into a guarantee. ★RE-WALKED AFTER THIS SESSION'S TWELVE PRODUCT FIXES so the evidence carries digests of the code as it now stands - R4b expired the prior rows because the fixes changed the very functions they rested on. Re-WALKED, never re-baselined.

control.note: the trigger handle_community_post_xp writes the award ledger, so a detector that cannot see this link cannot see any link

evidence.asserts: A multi-row or multi-table write either lands whole or not at all; a half-applied write is visible as an inconsistency in the ledger. Proven by a registered gate rather than a session - write_atomicity exercises every declared ledger invariant live, inside BEGIN/ROLLBACK, and checks that the paired halves of a write cannot come apart.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: PASS - every declared ledger invariant holds against the live database, exercised transactionally rather than reasoned about. The exposure the gate reports rather than hides is the honest part: 11 pages sequence TWO writes client-side, which is structural risk (a tab closed between them leaves the second undone) and is recorded as exposure, not counted as a failure, because no half-write has actually occurred in the data. That distinction is the same one this platform learned the hard way from a one-sided ledger write that passed every guard - the difference between "this could come apart" and "this has come apart" decides whether you are hardening a path or repairing rows. depends_on names the subject artifacts as well as the prover, so a migration or function under this claim still expires it, and replay re-earns it in one command instead of a browser session.
evidence.value_checked:
gate:write_atomicity (registered) | PASS: every declared ledger invariant holds live, exercised in BEGIN/ROLLBACK | 11 pages sequence two client-side writes - reported as structural exposure, not failed; no half-write present in the data
 | depends_on: tools/prove_write_atomicity.py

evidence.asserts: when this page's reads fail in this way, it renders a FAILURE the person can act on - never an emptiness, a stuck skeleton, or silence
evidence.checked: PASSES: 17 call(s) failed and the page said so: "lls EN FIL Sign Out COULDN'T REFRESH We could not load your latest hive data. Ch". THE ORACLE IS A DIFFERENCE, NOT A STRING, inherited from the marketplace spec this extends: the page is read HEALTHY first, and a pass requires the failure wording to APPEAR - if the healthy render already said it, the words were always there and prove nothing, so the page is UNGRADED. A pass therefore means the page answered a broken read with something failure-shaped that it does not say when healthy. FOUR WAYS TO FAIL IT: rendering EMPTINESS ('no items', 'nothing here') for a failure - the two are indistinguishable to a person and one of them is a lie, and this platform shipped exactly that when public-feed's Retry answered 'No public posts yet' over 15 existing posts; leaving a SKELETON shimmering at someone whose data will never arrive; saying nothing at all; or being ungraded because the injection never fired. The vocabulary is IMPORTED from session_signals.mjs, harvested from this product's own sentences - the spec's own note is that an oracle recognising only its author's phrasing measures vocabulary, not behaviour. ★ THREE OF THE SEVEN MODES CARRY THEIR OWN PASS CONDITION, because 'did a failure message appear?' is the right question for only four of them, and using one assertion for all seven is how a family looks green while asserting the wrong thing on three of its members. fail_slow is a SUCCESSFUL read that is merely late: demanding a failure message there would be demanding a LIE. It must show the page is WORKING - a skeleton, spinner or busy state - and it is sampled MID-FLIGHT, at 2.5s of a 6s delay, because by the time the data lands the answer has been erased; a final-state read would score a page that showed a blank screen for six seconds identically to one that showed a skeleton. fail_null_field is not an error at all - the rows arrive and their non-id fields are null - so the only question is whether the page prints `null`, `undefined` or `NaN` at a person. The nulls are applied to the REAL response rather than to a synthesised one, so the test exercises the page's own schema instead of this prover's idea of it, and the match is word-bounded so 'Nullarbor' or a part code containing 'nan' cannot trip it. fail_partial is a 200 whose JSON does not parse - what a connection dropped mid-transfer actually looks like - and must read as a failure rather than as 'no rows'. WHAT THE NULL MODE ACTUALLY FOUND, verified page by page rather than inferred from a sweep line: three pages print a raw null at a person, and all three share ONE shape - a `|| fallback` present on one interpolation and missing on its NEIGHBOUR in the same template literal. inventory:1542 `Available: ${item.qty_on_hand} ${item.unit || 'pcs'}` renders OUT OF STOCK null pcs eight times: the UNIT fell back, the QUANTITY did not - the page guards the decoration and leaves the number a technician acts on unguarded. alert-hub:611 `shift ${brief.shift_date} · model ${brief.model_version || 'amc-v1'}` prints `shift null` while rendering `(no headline)` two lines later, so the idiom was in hand at the time. skillmatrix:854 `Primary: ${_profile.primary_skill} · ${WORKER_NAME}` prints `Primary: null · Leandro Marquez` - a raw null in a person's DISCIPLINE, beside their name, on the surface whose job is stating their qualifications. THE CONSEQUENCES DIFFER AND ARE NOT FLATTENED: a wrong quantity, a wrong claim about a person, a wrong shift on a supervisor's brief. One habit, three one-token corrections - not a design decision. HOW THE FAILURE IS INDUCED, and why the method is the hard part: every Supabase REST/RPC call is failed at window.fetch, patched via addInitScript so it is in place BEFORE any page script runs. That timing is the whole trick. tests/failure-injection.spec.ts records that replacing window.fetch AFTER load never fires, because supabase-js captures fetch when the CLIENT IS CONSTRUCTED - so it used page.route instead; this project separately learned that page.route is bypassed by a warm SERVICE WORKER serving from cache. Both are true, and the reconciliation is WHEN THE PATCH LANDS: an init script is not a late override, and it sits above the service worker rather than below it. THE INJECTION COUNTS ITS OWN HITS and a page where the counter reads zero is UNGRADED, never judged - because a failure-injection oracle that does not inject produces the most convincing false findings available: 'the page said nothing about the error' is exactly what a page with NO error would say. WHAT THIS ORACLE FOUND ON ITS FIRST RUN, and it was a hole in a fix made earlier the same day: the central transport notice hung off `.then(res => ...)`, so a REJECTED or ABORTED fetch - which never produces a res - skipped it entirely. Status-bearing failures (500/401) were covered; transport failures were not. Measured on logbook: 13 rejected reads, ZERO page errors, ZERO console errors, and not one word on screen - the page caught the rejection and dropped it, which is the '118 annotated empty-catch blocks across 11 pages' habit utils.js already documents. FIXED at the transport in a `.catch` that NOTICES AND RE-THROWS, because that wrapper's own comment forbids a catch that swallows the error callers must surface; `throw err` leaves every caller's {data, error} untouched. Timeout and offline get DIFFERENT sentences, since 'check your connection' is useless advice for one and the only useful advice for the other; the connection notice IS cleared by the next successful read (the network is demonstrably back) while the permission notice deliberately is not. THREE INSTRUMENT CORRECTIONS BEHIND THIS ROW, each of which had produced a confident false FAIL. (1) The first version waited 9s for a timeout the platform bounds at 15s (whQueryTimeout, utils.js:1785) - measuring its own impatience and reporting 'the page said NOTHING', a true statement about an instant nobody experiences. (2) Widening the wait revealed that whQueryTimeout is adopted by only SIX surfaces (community, public-feed and the four marketplace pages), so on these 20 pages the only bound is the transport abort at WH_DB_TIMEOUT_MS || 45000; rather than idle 45s per page the prover sets that documented knob to 4s, which utils.js:703 explicitly invites ('tune via window.WH_DB_TIMEOUT_MS'). (3) The hang stub IGNORED THE ABORT SIGNAL, so the platform's own timeout became a no-op and the page sat silent forever - the stub was suppressing the exact mechanism under test. A fake fetch must emulate CANCELLATION, not just latency. SCOPE: V1 only - the page as it loads, signed in as supervisor - across all seven CC modes. The V2 view is a separate row and is NOT claimed here. community and public-feed are excluded because tests/failure-injection.spec.ts already walks them. NON-WRITING: only reads are failed; nothing is typed or submitted.

findings.title: NOT BANKED - fail_401: an expired session is not surfaced honestly on this page. THIS FAILS ON 17 OF 17 PAGES WALKED, and the fix is ADOPTION, not a new message
findings.detail: FAILURE STATES ARE INJECTED, never waited for. failures() intercepts the page's own reads and answers them with the failure under test, then reads what the page TELLS A PERSON. Every mutating verb is answered by a stub rather than forwarded - decided by blockWrite across the WHOLE Supabase surface, rpc and edge functions included - so nothing reaches the shared test database. The path is verified unchanged across the injection, and the surface is asserted before it: an expired session earlier today made 19 of 22 pages return identical landing-page readings, and 3 pages were REFUSED by that guard on this very sweep rather than measured. The navigation fence held on 16 of 16 pages read. THE ORACLE IS WHAT THE READER IS TOLD, not whether an error was caught. A caught error that renders nothing is indistinguishable, from the reader's side, from success. Stamped ::v=3: the top-level digest is a SET of per-statement content hashes, so a shared-library append expires nothing while a modify or delete correctly expires. Self-tested 8/8. FINDING: Injecting a 401 into this page's reads, the page does not tell the reader their session expired, does not name the session as the cause, and does not state the consequence for what they were doing. THE REFLEX IS TO WRITE THE MISSING MESSAGE AND THAT WOULD BE WRONG - it already exists. utils.js:1568 reads 'Your session expired, so nothing was saved. Sign in again and redo this step.' and :1611 has the read equivalent, with _WH_PG_DENIAL at :1518 and a careful 401-versus-403 note beneath it. There is even a comment recording that this was fixed once on the inquiry path, where a 42501 told a SIGNED-IN buyer their session had expired, and that 'the shared helper kept the bug for every other path'. Writing a new string would add a second source of truth for text that is already correct. SO THE DEFECT IS ADOPTION: the read path catches the status and never renders whReadError's text. A uniform 17-of-17 failure is not seventeen independent lapses, it is one shared path swallowing the status - which means ONE fix earns all seventeen rows in a single sweep. Same shape as the other platform-wide finds in this arc: ::placeholder absent everywhere, companion-launcher.js with no prefers-reduced-motion block at all. AND THE PROBE IS NOT AT FAULT, which matters before acting on a 17/17 result: fail_null_field passes on 16 of 16 pages under the same injection harness. A broken probe does not pass one injection everywhere and fail another everywhere. Row stays owed; measure adoption at the point of RENDER, not by the helper's existence.

findings.title: RETRACTED - the fail_timeout failure I recorded here was MY main-scoped text read missing a body-level notice, not a defect on this page
findings.detail: RETRACTED - THIS WAS MY INSTRUMENT, NOT THIS PAGE. I recorded fail_timeout failing on 11 of 16 pages and fail_partial on 13 of 16, described them as pages that say nothing on a timeout and present a partial result as complete, and wrote per-page findings saying so. All four CC oracles now pass on 12 of 12 pages, and NOTHING was changed on any timeout or partial code path in between. What changed is the PROBE: its text scope was document.querySelector('main'), and these pages render their failure messages into toasts, banners and live regions - which are fixed-position and therefore direct children of <body>, because a fixed element inside a transformed or overflow-clipped ancestor positions against that ancestor instead of the viewport. main.innerText could never contain them. So the pages were speaking and the probe was deaf. HOW I FOUND IT, and why it is worth recording rather than quietly re-banking: I added a central 401 notice at getDb()'s transport seam, VERIFIED it rendering - the element was in the DOM carrying the text - and fail_401 still read every sub-assertion false. That contradiction is what exposed the scope bug. The failure oracle now reads main PLUS live/alert/notice containers, deduped, and deliberately NOT all of body, because nav and hub chrome carry standing words like 'offline' and 'retry' that would forge a pass on every page. WHAT SURVIVES: the fail_401 finding was REAL. Before the central fix there was no session notice on any page at all - no element existed to be missed - so 12 of 12 pages genuinely told a reader nothing when their session died, and the fix at getDb() is what created the notice they now show. That one is not withdrawn. Only the timeout and partial claims are, and they are withdrawn in full. THE LESSON IS THE ONE THIS ARC KEEPS RE-LEARNING: an instrument that measures the wrong REGION produces well-formed readings, and a uniform failure across many pages should raise suspicion of the probe before it is written up as a platform defect. The same lens-scope error once measured 15 of 518 nodes for contrast because it scoped to <main> while the report mounted outside it.
findings.observed: fail_timeout now passes over 8 intercepted reads with no change to any timeout or partial code path; only the probe text scope changed

findings.detail: FAILURE STATES ARE INJECTED, never waited for. failures() intercepts the page's own reads and answers them with the failure under test, then reads what the page TELLS A PERSON. Every mutating verb is answered by a stub rather than forwarded - decided by blockWrite across the WHOLE Supabase surface, rpc and edge functions included - so nothing reaches the shared test database. The path is verified unchanged across the injection, and the surface is asserted before it: an expired session earlier today made 19 of 22 pages return identical landing-page readings, and 3 pages were REFUSED by that guard on this very sweep rather than measured. The navigation fence held on 16 of 16 pages read. THE ORACLE IS WHAT THE READER IS TOLD, not whether an error was caught. A caught error that renders nothing is indistinguishable, from the reader's side, from success. Stamped ::v=3: the top-level digest is a SET of per-statement content hashes, so a shared-library append expires nothing while a modify or delete correctly expires. Self-tested 8/8. FINDING: Under a truncated payload this page keeps what arrived - correct, and why keptSomething passes - but never tells the reader part of the data is missing. The rendered length came back byte-identical to the healthy baseline, which is the proof: an incomplete answer is shown as a whole one. 13 of 16 pages swept fail this. findings.title: RETRACTED - the fail_partial failure I recorded here was MY main-scoped text read missing a body-level notice, not a defect on this page
findings.detail: RETRACTED - THIS WAS MY INSTRUMENT, NOT THIS PAGE. I recorded fail_timeout failing on 11 of 16 pages and fail_partial on 13 of 16, described them as pages that say nothing on a timeout and present a partial result as complete, and wrote per-page findings saying so. All four CC oracles now pass on 12 of 12 pages, and NOTHING was changed on any timeout or partial code path in between. What changed is the PROBE: its text scope was document.querySelector('main'), and these pages render their failure messages into toasts, banners and live regions - which are fixed-position and therefore direct children of <body>, because a fixed element inside a transformed or overflow-clipped ancestor positions against that ancestor instead of the viewport. main.innerText could never contain them. So the pages were speaking and the probe was deaf. HOW I FOUND IT, and why it is worth recording rather than quietly re-banking: I added a central 401 notice at getDb()'s transport seam, VERIFIED it rendering - the element was in the DOM carrying the text - and fail_401 still read every sub-assertion false. That contradiction is what exposed the scope bug. The failure oracle now reads main PLUS live/alert/notice containers, deduped, and deliberately NOT all of body, because nav and hub chrome carry standing words like 'offline' and 'retry' that would forge a pass on every page. WHAT SURVIVES: the fail_401 finding was REAL. Before the central fix there was no session notice on any page at all - no element existed to be missed - so 12 of 12 pages genuinely told a reader nothing when their session died, and the fix at getDb() is what created the notice they now show. That one is not withdrawn. Only the timeout and partial claims are, and they are withdrawn in full. THE LESSON IS THE ONE THIS ARC KEEPS RE-LEARNING: an instrument that measures the wrong REGION produces well-formed readings, and a uniform failure across many pages should raise suspicion of the probe before it is written up as a platform defect. The same lens-scope error once measured 15 of 518 nodes for contrast because it scoped to <main> while the report mounted outside it.

findings.title: RETRACTION SUPERSEDED - the withdrawal above rested on a contaminated reading; fail_partial genuinely FAILS here (9 of 12 pages), reinstated
findings.detail: THE RETRACTION ON THIS ROW WAS ITSELF WRONG, and this note supersedes it. Three measurements of fail_partial exist and only the middle one is contaminated: (1) FIRST READ, text scope = <main>: failed on 13 of 16 pages. (2) SECOND READ, after I widened the scope to include body-level notice regions: passed on 12 of 12 - and on the strength of that I retracted the finding on 12 pages, writing that 'the pages were speaking and the probe was deaf'. (3) THIRD READ, after I made my own 401 notice CLEAR ITSELF: fails on 9 of 12. NOTHING ON ANY PARTIAL CODE PATH CHANGED ACROSS THOSE THREE. What changed in (2) is that the central session notice I had just added to getDb() was still pinned to the page from the 401 injection earlier in the same failures() run, so namesTheFailure was matching MY OWN leftover text - 'Your session expired, so this page could not be loaded' - rather than anything the page said about a truncated payload. Reading (1) and reading (3) AGREE with each other; (2) is the outlier, and (2) is the one I acted on. SO THE ORIGINAL FINDING STANDS, at 9 of 12 rather than 13 of 16: on this page a truncated payload is rendered without the reader being told part of the data is missing. The withdrawal note above should be read as evidence about my instrument's history, not as an exoneration of this page. findings.detail: FAILS: 20 call(s) failed and the page said NOTHING about it (1098 chars healthy -> 951 chars failed). THE ORACLE IS A DIFFERENCE, NOT A STRING, inherited from the marketplace spec this extends: the page is read HEALTHY first, and a pass requires the failure wording to APPEAR - if the healthy render already said it, the words were always there and prove nothing, so the page is UNGRADED. A pass therefore means the page answered a broken read with something failure-shaped that it does not say when healthy. FOUR WAYS TO FAIL IT: rendering EMPTINESS ('no items', 'nothing here') for a failure - the two are indistinguishable to a person and one of them is a lie, and this platform shipped exactly that when public-feed's Retry answered 'No public posts yet' over 15 existing posts; leaving a SKELETON shimmering at someone whose data will never arrive; saying nothing at all; or being ungraded because the injection never fired. The vocabulary is IMPORTED from session_signals.mjs, harvested from this product's own sentences - the spec's own note is that an oracle recognising only its author's phrasing measures vocabulary, not behaviour. ★ THREE OF THE SEVEN MODES CARRY THEIR OWN PASS CONDITION, because 'did a failure message appear?' is the right question for only four of them, and using one assertion for all seven is how a family looks green while asserting the wrong thing on three of its members. fail_slow is a SUCCESSFUL read that is merely late: demanding a failure message there would be demanding a LIE. It must show the page is WORKING - a skeleton, spinner or busy state - and it is sampled MID-FLIGHT, at 2.5s of a 6s delay, because by the time the data lands the answer has been erased; a final-state read would score a page that showed a blank screen for six seconds identically to one that showed a skeleton. fail_null_field is not an error at all - the rows arrive and their non-id fields are null - so the only question is whether the page prints `null`, `undefined` or `NaN` at a person. The nulls are applied to the REAL response rather than to a synthesised one, so the test exercises the page's own schema instead of this prover's idea of it, and the match is word-bounded so 'Nullarbor' or a part code containing 'nan' cannot trip it. fail_partial is a 200 whose JSON does not parse - what a connection dropped mid-transfer actually looks like - and must read as a failure rather than as 'no rows'. WHAT THE NULL MODE ACTUALLY FOUND, verified page by page rather than inferred from a sweep line: three pages print a raw null at a person, and all three share ONE shape - a `|| fallback` present on one interpolation and missing on its NEIGHBOUR in the same template literal. inventory:1542 `Available: ${item.qty_on_hand} ${item.unit || 'pcs'}` renders OUT OF STOCK null pcs eight times: the UNIT fell back, the QUANTITY did not - the page guards the decoration and leaves the number a technician acts on unguarded. alert-hub:611 `shift ${brief.shift_date} · model ${brief.model_version || 'amc-v1'}` prints `shift null` while rendering `(no headline)` two lines later, so the idiom was in hand at the time. skillmatrix:854 `Primary: ${_profile.primary_skill} · ${WORKER_NAME}` prints `Primary: null · Leandro Marquez` - a raw null in a person's DISCIPLINE, beside their name, on the surface whose job is stating their qualifications. THE CONSEQUENCES DIFFER AND ARE NOT FLATTENED: a wrong quantity, a wrong claim about a person, a wrong shift on a supervisor's brief. One habit, three one-token corrections - not a design decision. HOW THE FAILURE IS INDUCED, and why the method is the hard part: every Supabase REST/RPC call is failed at window.fetch, patched via addInitScript so it is in place BEFORE any page script runs. That timing is the whole trick. tests/failure-injection.spec.ts records that replacing window.fetch AFTER load never fires, because supabase-js captures fetch when the CLIENT IS CONSTRUCTED - so it used page.route instead; this project separately learned that page.route is bypassed by a warm SERVICE WORKER serving from cache. Both are true, and the reconciliation is WHEN THE PATCH LANDS: an init script is not a late override, and it sits above the service worker rather than below it. THE INJECTION COUNTS ITS OWN HITS and a page where the counter reads zero is UNGRADED, never judged - because a failure-injection oracle that does not inject produces the most convincing false findings available: 'the page said nothing about the error' is exactly what a page with NO error would say. WHAT THIS ORACLE FOUND ON ITS FIRST RUN, and it was a hole in a fix made earlier the same day: the central transport notice hung off `.then(res => ...)`, so a REJECTED or ABORTED fetch - which never produces a res - skipped it entirely. Status-bearing failures (500/401) were covered; transport failures were not. Measured on logbook: 13 rejected reads, ZERO page errors, ZERO console errors, and not one word on screen - the page caught the rejection and dropped it, which is the '118 annotated empty-catch blocks across 11 pages' habit utils.js already documents. FIXED at the transport in a `.catch` that NOTICES AND RE-THROWS, because that wrapper's own comment forbids a catch that swallows the error callers must surface; `throw err` leaves every caller's {data, error} untouched. Timeout and offline get DIFFERENT sentences, since 'check your connection' is useless advice for one and the only useful advice for the other; the connection notice IS cleared by the next successful read (the network is demonstrably back) while the permission notice deliberately is not. THREE INSTRUMENT CORRECTIONS BEHIND THIS ROW, each of which had produced a confident false FAIL. (1) The first version waited 9s for a timeout the platform bounds at 15s (whQueryTimeout, utils.js:1785) - measuring its own impatience and reporting 'the page said NOTHING', a true statement about an instant nobody experiences. (2) Widening the wait revealed that whQueryTimeout is adopted by only SIX surfaces (community, public-feed and the four marketplace pages), so on these 20 pages the only bound is the transport abort at WH_DB_TIMEOUT_MS || 45000; rather than idle 45s per page the prover sets that documented knob to 4s, which utils.js:703 explicitly invites ('tune via window.WH_DB_TIMEOUT_MS'). (3) The hang stub IGNORED THE ABORT SIGNAL, so the platform's own timeout became a no-op and the page sat silent forever - the stub was suppressing the exact mechanism under test. A fake fetch must emulate CANCELLATION, not just latency. SCOPE: V1 only - the page as it loads, signed in as supervisor - across all seven CC modes. The V2 view is a separate row and is NOT claimed here. community and public-feed are excluded because tests/failure-injection.spec.ts already walks them. NON-WRITING: only reads are failed; nothing is typed or submitted.

evidence.asserts: Holds now, after fixing one tile that would have lied at scale. get_hive_dashboard is careful about this nearly everywhere: open jobs and risks each return a top-5 detail list AND a separate uncapped count, so the tile shows the true number while the payload stays small, and pm_overdue_count does the same. Low stock was the exception - it returned low_stock_items capped at LIMIT 100 with no count, and index.html:4342 rendered `num: lowStock.length`. The function's own comment states the mechanism ('the client derives BOTH the tile count (.length) AND the out-of-stock candidate from this array') and is silent about the consequence: past 100 low parts the tile stops counting and reads exactly 100, for any hive, forever. It bites nobody today - the busiest hive has 3 low-stock rows - so this was a latent defect fixed on principle: a cap is not a count, and a tile that silently saturates is precisely the 'tile outlives its query' shape this invariant names. The 100-row array is unchanged, because the client still needs the ROWS to derive the out-of-stock subset; only the tile's number now comes from a real total, with a fallback to the array length so a deployment without the new field renders something rather than nothing.

subject.name: multi-hive resolves to ONE hive, everywhere

scenarios.oracle: a multi-hive worker resolves to exactly one hive deterministically, and the tiles all name the SAME one - the .maybeSingle()/limit(1) class that bounced multi-hive users before

evidence.asserts: FIXED THIS WALK. The half of this invariant that has bitten before was already safe: the page reads ALL of a worker's memberships (.limit(500), no .maybeSingle(), no .limit(1)), so a multi-hive worker is not bounced. The half that was open is the one the oracle actually names - DETERMINISTICALLY. The page selected the active tenant with `const first = hives[0]` from a query carrying no ORDER BY, and v_hives_truth has none internally either, so which hive a two-hive worker landed in was left to whatever order the planner happened to return. Every tile then follows that choice, so the whole dashboard silently agrees on a tenant nobody chose. Two such workers exist in this data (Christine Dizon and Pablo Aguilar), so this is a real population, not a hypothetical. Two changes: the query is ordered by name then id, making the order TOTAL so two hives sharing a name cannot swap; and the pick now prefers wh_active_hive_id when the worker is still a member of it, because a deterministic sort ALONE would be stable while quietly moving someone to whichever hive sorts first, rather than the one they were working in.
evidence.checked: HONEST LIMIT, stated rather than dressed up: I could NOT make the unordered order flip on demand. A rewriting UPDATE on one of Christine Dizon's two hives returned the same sequence on both passes, so no empirical instability was observed. The defect is the missing GUARANTEE, not an observed flip - an unordered SELECT has no defined order, and this one feeds a tenant choice, so it can change with a plan change, a vacuum or concurrency without anything in the code changing. Confirmed the view itself supplies no ordering (pg_get_viewdef contains no ORDER BY), which is what rules out the 'it is sorted anyway' reading. Confirmed the new key is total across the live rows - (name, id) is distinct for every hive - so the sort cannot leave two rows interchangeable. Verified the multi-hive population is non-empty first, since an invariant about multi-hive workers proved over zero of them would be vacuous.

findings.title: MEASURED with tools/prove_source_chip.mjs, live: 41 views graded across the roster - 18 make a TRUE provenance claim, 23 make NO claim, 0 name a feed they never read.
findings.detail: MEASURED with tools/prove_source_chip.mjs, live: 41 views graded across the roster - 18 make a TRUE provenance claim, 23 make NO claim, 0 name a feed they never read. THE ORACLE MATTERS MORE THAN MOST UI TEXT: a source chip is a promise that a number came from named feeds, and a reader uses it to decide whether to trust the figure. A chip naming a feed the page never queried is worse than no chip, because it manufactures confidence. SO THE CLAIM IS CHECKED AGAINST THE NETWORK, not the source: every PostgREST /rest/v1/<relation> the view actually requests is captured at runtime, and each schema-shaped token the chip names must correspond to one. It is deliberately ONE-DIRECTIONAL - a chip that SUMMARISES is fine, a chip that INVENTS is not. ★TWO MANUFACTURED FINDINGS WERE CAUGHT AND REMOVED BEFORE ANY OF THIS WAS BANKED. The first version of the token test counted the bare word `logbook`, so asset-hub and analytics were both reported as naming an unread feed - on the strength of ordinary prose: 'Based on your asset records, risk scores, logbook, failure analysis'. That is a sentence describing FEATURES to a person, not an assertion about a table, and analytics is right on its own terms - it reads analytics_snapshots, a snapshot DERIVED from logbook data, which is precisely what 'saved snapshot ... based on your logbook' says. A keyword match over human prose is how a page's own helper text becomes a defect. The test now counts a token only when it is unmistakably schema-shaped (a v_ prefix, a _truth suffix, or a known table prefix + underscore); bare English words never qualify. ★AND THE VIEW IS READ INSIDE ITSELF. V1 is graded at page scope and V2 inside the OPENED view via the shared tools/dialog_targets.mjs registry, because crediting a V2 row with a V1 reading is the one-measurement-swept-two-views error this bank has already paid for once. NOT BANKED GREEN: this view displays NO source chip at all (0 on screen while the surface requested 7 relation(s)). A surface that makes no provenance claim has not made a TRUE one, and the oracle asks whether the claim is true - so silence cannot satisfy it. Scoring it green would credit the absence of a promise as a kept promise. THIS IS ALSO NOT AUTOMATICALLY A DEFECT. Most of the 23 are V2 dialogs - a composer, a confirm sheet, a detail panel - which display a form rather than a derived figure, and a provenance chip on a surface that states no number would be noise. WHAT SETTLES IT is the per-view question the bank actually asks: does THIS view show a figure a reader would want provenance for? If yes, the chip is missing and this is a real finding; if no, the row is declared-na under R10 with 'this view states no derived figure' as the reason and the CM comprehension oracles as its replacement. Left owed rather than guessed, because that question is per-view and answering it from a count would be inventing the verdict.

Most numbers on this platform are COUNTS - 9 open jobs, 28 PMs overdue - and a count has no unit to show; flagging those would redden every surface, and a check that reddens everything is measuring itself. So 'MTBF: 45' fails, 'MTBF: 45 days' passes, and 'Open Jobs: 9' is never asked. ★THIS VIEW RENDERED ZERO DIMENSION-LABELLED QUANTITIES ON ITS DEFAULT STATE, so the check ABSTAINS rather than passing. '0 failing' over 0 judged is exactly the vacuous green this bank exists to refuse - it would read identically to a page that had been thoroughly checked. ★THE INSTRUMENT WAS WRONG TWICE BEFORE IT WAS RIGHT, both caught by disbelieving the output. (1) It first accepted only BARE digits, so any value already carrying its unit never entered the set - 21 of 22 pages reported '0 judged' on a platform that renders MTBF and OEE nearly everywhere. An implausible abstention is an instrument fault, not a finding. (2) It then failed analytics on 'total downtime = 717.9h' because the time vocabulary listed hr/hrs/hours but not a bare 'h'. An oracle's vocabulary IS the oracle. Both are fixed and recorded in the tool. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: drive this page's V2/V3 views open before scanning - the quantities that owe units here live behind a modal, a tab or a selected record, exactly as effect_visible needed the disclosure and the selection performed before it could see anything.

findings.detail: MEASURED with tools/prove_number_explained.mjs (new) - on the rendered page, in the view that owns the metric. ★NAMING IS NOT EXPLAINING, which is why this is a separate prover from prove_number_labelled.mjs. That one asks whether something adjacent NAMES the figure and the roster passes it 79/79. This asks whether a person can say what the number MEANS: 'PM compliance 61%%' is named and unexplained - 61%% of WHAT, over WHAT window, counted HOW? ★ONLY DERIVED FIGURES OWE AN EXPLANATION, and getting that wrong would redden every surface. A raw COUNT explains itself - 'Open Jobs 9' is nine jobs. A PERCENTAGE, RATE, SCORE, INDEX or COMPOSITE is computed from things the reader cannot see, and that is where the meaning lives off-screen. Any ONE of a denominator, a window, a derivation or a definition discharges the obligation; requiring all four would fail good surfaces. ★THE INSTRUMENT WAS WRONG THREE TIMES BEFORE IT WAS RIGHT, each caught by disbelieving the output: (1) EIGHTEEN abstentions on a platform that renders OEE and MTBF - analytics' KPI heroes live behind its phase panels, not the landing view, so the prover now reaches the view that owns the metric; (2) it failed hive's 'HEALTHY /100 composite risk - lower is better', a figure that states its scale AND its direction, because my denominator pattern demanded a digit on BOTH sides of the slash; (3) it failed project-report on 'Replace mechanical seal + bearings Leandro Mar... = 4.0' because the enclosing block resolved to a whole TABLE and every cell inherited the section's derived-ness - adjacency is not several hundred characters of table, so table cells are now excluded and long labels skipped. FOR THIS PAGE: no DERIVED figure rendered in the view measured - its numbers are raw counts, which explain themselves. Recorded as an ABSTENTION, not a pass: '0 unexplained of 0' reads identically to a thorough check, which is the vacuous green this bank refuses.

evidence.checked: MEASURED LIVE on the signed-in ops-home, then settled against psql as postgres. The three KPI tiles read: Open Jobs 9, PM Overdue 28, Low Stock 3. Against the database for this hive: 9 open logbook entries hive-wide, 28 distinct PM assets with an overdue scope item, and 3 items flagged is_low_stock over the approved/pending/rejected set. All three agree. ★AND THIS IS THE FOURTH SURFACE CARRYING THE SAME THREE FACTS, which is what makes index worth checking rather than assuming. PM Overdue 28 now reads identically on index, hive (#ss-pm-hero), pm-scheduler (#stat-overdue) and shift-brain (#sb-pms-hero). Low Stock 3 reads identically on index, hive, inventory and shift-brain. Open Jobs 9 matches hive's #stat-open and shift-brain's carry count - and note it is the HIVE-WIDE figure (9), not the signed-in worker's own (6, which is what logbook's pill correctly shows). Four copies of one number is four chances for one of them to be left behind by a predicate change, and nothing on any of the four screens would look wrong. DISCRIMINATION, measured this session rather than assumed: the low-stock figure reads 3 under the reorder-point rule and 0 under a naive qty<=1 threshold, so a regression to a hardcoded threshold on ANY of the four surfaces breaks the set. The open-jobs figure reads 9 hive-wide and 6 worker-scoped, so a mis-scoped read is visible as a 9-vs-6 disagreement rather than hiding. PM overdue is bounded by the hive's 30 PM assets. WORTH RECORDING ABOUT THIS PAGE SPECIFICALLY: index is two products behind one URL - an inline script sets html.wh-signed-in before <body> parses, so an anon visitor gets the marketing landing and a signed-in one gets this dashboard. These tiles do not exist for the anon view at all, which is why the count oracle for V1 has a subject only in the signed-in state, and why a walk that did not establish a session would have found nothing here and could easily have recorded 'no numbers on this page' as a fact about the page rather than about the walk.

evidence.asserts: FIXED THIS WALK, on a live browser. ops-home carries no half-fillable sheet, so the oracle's substance on V1 is the other half of its sentence: after a reload the surface must return to a TRUTHFUL state. It did not. Reloaded with an expired session, the page rendered two statements at once - 'Your session ended. These numbers were not read. This is not an all-clear: nothing here was loaded with your account' and, directly beneath it, 'ALL CLEAR - Nothing urgent right now.' The banner named the exact misreading its neighbour then committed, on the screen a supervisor uses to decide whether the plant needs them today. The cure was already written and could not arm itself: the guard at index.html:4628 reads `if (!pick && _signalsUnread.length)` and renders a proper 'Could not check / This is not an all-clear' card, with a long comment explaining why an empty variable must not become an established fact. But _signalsUnread is only ever populated on the LEGACY per-query path; on the RPC path it stays [], so in this state the guard's own condition was false. The verdict now also defers to the session-dead banner, a second and independent signal that the reads did not happen, which was sitting in the DOM unconsulted.
evidence.checked: Both states observed in a real browser against a locally served page, not inferred. Before: session-dead banner present AND 'ALL CLEAR' present on the same screen. After: same precondition re-established and confirmed present (session_dead_banner=true, ops-home visibly on screen), 'ALL CLEAR' absent, 'not an all-clear' retained. Waiting for the banner before reading the verdict is what makes the after-reading meaningful - an intermediate run where the banner never appeared was DISCARDED rather than counted, because a verdict read without the precondition proves nothing about a fix conditioned on it. That run also explained itself: the session-dead path clears wh_last_worker, so the identity has to be re-set before each reproduction, which is why the second attempt silently fell back to the marketing view. Also confirmed the signed-in swap is atomic on reload - html.wh-signed-in stamped, ops-home block, mkt-wrap none, never both and never neither.

evidence.asserts: repeating an identical write does not create a second record, and the guarantee is enforced by a constraint rather than by the client
evidence.checked: PROVEN BY REPEATING THE WRITE, inside BEGIN ... ROLLBACK as an authenticated member. The same row - same primary key, same payload - was inserted twice in one transaction. The second attempt was refused: 'duplicate key value violates unique constraint logbook_pkey'. So a repeat cannot create a second record, and the guarantee comes from a CONSTRAINT rather than from client-side de-duplication that a double-tap, a retry, or an offline queue drain could outrun. WHY THE CONSTRAINT IS THE RIGHT PLACE FOR IT: this platform queues field-capture writes offline and drains them on reconnect, so the same logical write can genuinely arrive twice from two directions. A uniqueness guarantee that lives in the page dies with the page's assumptions; one that lives in the index holds for the queue drain, the retry and the second tab alike. VERIFIED CLEAN: 0 probe rows survived. ANCHORED ON supabase/migrations PER A13. SCOPE: this settles the REPEAT of an identical write. It does not settle a second write with a DIFFERENT client-generated id representing the same intent - that is the offline-queue collapse question and lives on its own seam row.

Its sentence says 'try again' but there is no CONTROL to do so - the words invite an action the page does not offer. THE PATTERN EXISTS ON THIS PLATFORM, so this is adoption: achievements renders a Retry button beside its toast, and public-feed's Retry was measured firing a real re-request and then rendering 15 post cards. Only 2 of 22 pages have one. WHAT WOULD PASS IT: a control that RE-ISSUES the failed read - the probe counts requests fired after the click, so a button that merely re-renders the previous failure fails too. That is the exact defect commit 3ddef99d fixed on public-feed. MEASURED BY ANSWERING EVERY READ WITH A 500 AT window.fetch AND READING WHAT THE PAGE SAYS NEXT. Each `/rest/v1/` and `/rpc/` request resolves to a synthetic `{"code":"500"}` with Content-Type application/json; `/auth/v1/` is untouched so the session survives, which is what makes this a SERVER fault rather than a dead network. Interceptions are counted and a verdict over zero failed reads is refused as vacuous. Every claim below quotes the page's own visible sentence, collected from leaf-ish elements under a composed-visibility test (getClientRects + checkVisibility + an ancestor walk for display/visibility/opacity) so hidden template copy cannot be mistaken for something a reader sees. TWO EARLIER VERSIONS OF THIS SWEEP WERE THROWN AWAY, WHICH IS WHY THE NUMBERS HERE ARE TRUSTED. The first used Playwright's `route()` and intercepted **0** requests on all 8 pages while they rendered live data - a registered service worker sits between page and transport in a warm context, so route() never saw the calls. The second omitted the identity guard and returned byte-identical output for seven different pages (14,677 chars of marketing copy) because the session had expired and every page had redirected to `index.html?signin=1`. This version guards INSIDE the evaluate: expected uid, `location.pathname` ends in the page's own file, and body chars outside the 13,000-16,000 landing band - refusing rather than reporting. PLATFORM RESULT, all 22 pages: **9 state the failure in domain language** (hive, inventory, dayplanner, pm-scheduler, index, skillmatrix, achievements, voice-journal, assistant) and **11 say nothing or assert a falsehood**.
